title: Vesalius and the Renaissance return to dissection
text:
CHAPTER 1. EARLIEST IDEAS ABOUT THE BRAIN
SECTION 1.4. VESALIUS AND THE RENAISSANCE RETURN TO DISSECTION

From reading anatomy to doing anatomy

By the fifteenth century, human dissection had returned to some European universities, especially in Italy. Mondino de Luzzi in Bologna had performed public dissections in the early fourteenth century and wrote a short anatomy manual (the Anathomia, around 1316) that was used for a long time. But teaching remained heavily textual. The authority of Galen, often filtered through Arabic and Latin commentaries, framed what students expected to see.

Two developments of the Renaissance changed this. First, artists became interested in accurate depiction of the human body. Leonardo da Vinci (1452 to 1519) dissected human bodies and made extraordinary anatomical drawings. For the brain, he is known for making a wax cast of the ventricles of an ox brain, by injecting molten wax and then removing the surrounding tissue, which gave him a more accurate picture of their three-dimensional shape. Leonardo's anatomical notebooks were not published in his lifetime, however, and had little influence on the science of his day. Second, printing made it possible to reproduce detailed images exactly, so that an accurate drawing could reach every reader in the same form. A manuscript copied by hand degrades with each copy; a woodblock print does not.

Andreas Vesalius brought these developments together.

Andreas Vesalius

Andreas Vesalius was born in Brussels in 1514 into a family of physicians and pharmacists to the imperial court. He studied at Leuven, then at Paris, where he trained in the Galenic tradition, and then went to Padua, one of the leading medical schools in Europe. He received his medical degree at Padua in 1537 and was appointed to teach surgery and anatomy there almost immediately, while still in his early twenties.

Vesalius changed how anatomy was taught. Instead of reading from a text while an assistant dissected, he performed dissections himself and taught directly from the body. He used drawings and charts in teaching and in 1538 published a set of six large anatomical sheets, the Tabulae anatomicae sex, some drawn with the artist Jan van Calcar. As he gained more experience with human bodies, he increasingly found places where Galen's descriptions did not match. He came to the view, now accepted, that many of Galen's errors arose because Galen had dissected animals, not people.

The Fabrica

In 1543 Vesalius published De humani corporis fabrica libri septem ("On the fabric of the human body in seven books"), printed in Basel by Johannes Oporinus. The same year saw the publication of Copernicus's De revolutionibus, and the two books are often paired as symbols of the beginning of the scientific revolution. Vesalius also prepared a shorter companion, the Epitome, for students.

The Fabrica is famous for its woodcut illustrations: skeletons and muscle men posed in landscapes, and detailed figures of organs. The artists are not named in the book, and the question of who drew them has been debated. Jan van Calcar and others from the workshop of Titian in Venice have been proposed, but the attribution is uncertain. The quality of the images was unprecedented, and they were widely copied (often without permission) across Europe.

The seventh book of the Fabrica deals with the brain. Vesalius presented a sequence of illustrations showing the brain as it is progressively sliced from the top down, horizontal section by horizontal section, revealing the ventricles, the corpus callosum, the basal structures, and so on. If you have seen a modern MRI scan as a series of slices, you will recognize the idea. Vesalius was producing a printed stack of sections, a kind of manual tomography.

Corrections to Galen

For the nervous system, several of Vesalius's points are notable:

- He did not find the rete mirabile in the human brain. He noted that it exists in some animals, such as sheep and oxen, but not in humans. Since Galen's theory of producing psychic pneuma relied on this structure, its absence was a significant problem for the theory, even though Vesalius did not abandon the general idea of spirits.
- He was skeptical of the medieval cell doctrine. He noted that the ventricles of humans and of other animals are similar, while humans have far greater reasoning abilities. If the ventricles produced reason, why should animals with similar ventricles lack it? This is an elegant comparative argument: if structure X is the same in species A and species B, but function Y differs, X probably does not explain Y.
- He described the brain's structures with much greater accuracy than his predecessors, including the corpus callosum, the fornix, the thalamus region, and the general arrangement of the ventricles, though some structures were described only roughly and much of the internal anatomy remained unclear.
- He was cautious about saying how the brain actually produces mental functions. He wrote, in effect, that he could follow the anatomy but could not see in it how the brain performs imagination, reasoning, and memory. This honesty about the limits of anatomy is worth remembering.

Vesalius also made errors, and some of Galen's ideas survived in his work. And he was not alone; other anatomists of the period, such as Realdo Colombo, Gabriele Falloppio (Fallopius), and Bartolomeo Eustachi (Eustachius), made important observations and corrected both Galen and Vesalius in places. But the Fabrica changed the standard for what anatomical knowledge should be: based on direct observation of human bodies, communicated by accurate images.

Vesalius's later life

After the Fabrica, Vesalius left academic life to become a court physician, first to the Holy Roman Emperor Charles V and then to Philip II of Spain. His work attracted criticism from Galenists, including his former teacher Jacobus Sylvius in Paris, who defended Galen fiercely. In 1564 Vesalius left on a pilgrimage to Jerusalem and died on the return journey on the Greek island of Zakynthos. The reasons for his pilgrimage have been the subject of various stories, but the documented facts are limited, and many of the dramatic stories are not reliable.

The next generations of brain anatomy

The century after Vesalius brought steady progress in brain anatomy. Some names to know:

- Costanzo Varolio (1543 to 1575) described the pons, which is still called the pons Varolii.
- Franciscus Sylvius (Franz de le Boe, 1614 to 1672, not to be confused with Jacobus Sylvius) is associated with the lateral sulcus, often called the Sylvian fissure, and with the cerebral aqueduct (aqueduct of Sylvius), though the history of these eponyms is somewhat tangled.
- Thomas Willis (1621 to 1675), an English physician at Oxford, published Cerebri anatome in 1664, with illustrations by the architect Christopher Wren. Willis described the circle of arteries at the base of the brain, now called the circle of Willis, and is credited with introducing the word "neurology" (in its Latin form) to the language. Importantly, Willis began to shift attention from the ventricles to the brain tissue itself. He proposed that different functions were associated with different solid parts of the brain, for example the cerebral cortex with memory and will, and the cerebellum with involuntary functions. These assignments are not accurate by modern standards, but the move from cavities to tissue was a critical conceptual step.

Why images matter

The Fabrica reminds us that science depends on representation. Before printing, descriptions of anatomy changed as manuscripts were copied. After printing, the same image could be studied by thousands of readers, criticized, and corrected. In modern neuroscience, the equivalent of the Fabrica is a shared digital atlas. Projects like the Allen Brain Atlas provide standardized reference brains and datasets so that a researcher in one lab can say "this neuron is located at these coordinates" and another researcher anywhere in the world knows exactly what is meant. Common coordinate frameworks for the mouse brain and standard spaces for the human brain, such as the MNI templates, serve the same purpose for imaging studies.

For you as an engineer, the comparison is with standardized technical drawings and CAD models. A part is not truly specified until there is a precise, shareable representation of it. Vesalius did for the human body what engineering drawing standards later did for machines.

Bridge to AI: datasets, benchmarks, and seeing for yourself

There are three useful parallels between the Vesalian revolution and modern AI.

First, the value of high-quality data. Vesalius's main advantage over Galen was not greater intelligence but better data: human bodies instead of monkeys and pigs. In machine learning, a model trained on data from the wrong distribution (for example, images of objects in clean studio lighting) will fail in the target domain (cluttered real-world scenes). This is called distribution shift. Galen's anatomy was, in effect, a model trained on animal data and deployed on humans. Many of its errors were distribution shift errors.

Second, the value of shared reference data. The Fabrica became a reference that others could check against. In AI, datasets such as ImageNet played a similar role for computer vision. A large shared dataset of labeled images made it possible to compare methods fairly, and progress on that benchmark helped drive the deep learning revolution in the early 2010s. Like the Fabrica, such datasets also carry errors and biases, which later researchers have to find and correct.

Third, the slicing approach. Vesalius showed the brain as a sequence of horizontal slices. Modern neuroimaging and connectomics do the same, but at vastly higher resolution, and machine learning is now essential for analyzing the slices. In electron microscopy connectomics, a brain is cut into thousands of extremely thin sections, each imaged, and convolutional neural networks are used to trace the outlines of neurons from slice to slice. In a striking loop, a technology loosely inspired by the visual cortex is now used to map the brain. We will return to this in the chapter on connectomics.

Summary

- Renaissance anatomy combined human dissection, artistic skill, and the printing press.
- Andreas Vesalius, teaching at Padua, dissected human bodies himself and published De humani corporis fabrica in 1543.
- The Fabrica's illustrations set a new standard, and its seventh book presented the brain in a series of horizontal sections.
- Vesalius showed that the rete mirabile is absent in humans and questioned the ventricular theory of mental faculties.
- Later anatomists, especially Thomas Willis, moved attention from the ventricles to the brain tissue.
- The importance of accurate, shared representations links the Fabrica to modern brain atlases and to datasets and benchmarks in AI.
